outcome: Garonzi and Margolis (arXiv:2509.25118) proved the Herzog-Schönheim conjecture for two classes of finite groups — finite simple groups and symmetric groups — settling these cases while the general conjecture (over arbitrary groups) remains open.
summary: The Herzog-Schönheim conjecture (1974) asks whether a coset partition of a group G by subgroups of finite index can have distinct indices; it conjectures the answer is no (some two indices must coincide). Since 26 Jan 2024, the main development is a preprint by Garonzi and Margolis, 'The Herzog-Schönheim conjecture for simple and symmetric groups' (arXiv:2509.25118, submitted 2025-09-29, revised 2026-05-05), which proves the conjecture holds for all finite simple groups and all finite symmetric groups. This is a genuine case of the stated problem — a restriction to specific classes of groups — not a variant, so it counts as `partial` per §3.1 (settling a case narrows the territory of the general conjecture, which remains open for groups in general, including e.g. general finite or infinite groups). I read the paper's full HTML text (not just the abstract): the authors state they 'rely on computer calculations' using GAP and Mathematica (standard computer-algebra systems, not AI per §6.2's exclusion of computer algebra/exhaustive search from AI codes) and thank three mathematicians (Roney-Dougal, Craven, Liebeck) for mathematical consultations on maximal subgroups of simple groups of Lie type, with Liebeck given credit for proving one proposition. No mention anywhere in the paper of AI, ML, LLMs, or any AI-assisted tooling. I also found and checked a July 2024 arXiv paper ('A Note on Finite Nilpotent Groups', arXiv:2407.05498) that surfaced under nilpotent-group searches; it does not concern the Herzog-Schönheim conjecture at all (different characterization of nilpotent groups), so it is irrelevant. I also found a paper on the conjecture for free groups using covering spaces that appeared in print in the journal Beiträge zur Algebra und Geometrie in April 2024 — but this is arXiv:1804.11103, a 2018 preprint by Chouraqui; the 2024 date is only the journal's print/online publication lag, which §6.3 explicitly says not to use for dating, so this is not a window event (it predates 26 Jan 2024 in substance). No counterexample or disproof of any case was found; no withdrawal or dispute was found.
competing_reading: One could argue that proving the conjecture for simple and symmetric groups is a large enough achievement, covering essentially all the 'hard' finite non-abelian building blocks, that it deserves more weight than a typical `partial` — but per §6.1 this is still a case of the problem, not a resolution of the general conjecture (which covers arbitrary, including infinite, groups), so `partial` is the correct code regardless of the result's significance.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) covering the fully general statement — all groups, or at least all finite groups — would move this to `resolved` or a status reflecting full resolution; a peer-reviewed/expert-digested version of the Garonzi-Margolis result would not change the status code but would strengthen confidence.
